blocks.explanation:
A "show that" question: both sides must come out equal.
Plan: write both terms on the left with factorials, take a common factor, and simplify to \({}^{21}C_{7}\). A numerical check follows.
steps:
Given: \({}^{20}C_{7} + {}^{20}C_{6}\).
To show: it equals \({}^{21}C_{7}\).
Method: \({}^{n}C_{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\); make the denominators the same, then add.

Make the denominators equal
\[\dfrac{20!}{7!\,13!} = \dfrac{20! \cdot 14}{7!\,14!}\]
\[\dfrac{20!}{6!\,14!} = \dfrac{20! \cdot 7}{7!\,14!}\]
Why: \(14! = 14 \cdot 13!\) and \(7! = 7 \cdot 6!\), so we multiply top and bottom by 14 and by 7.

Recognise the result
\[\dfrac{21!}{7!\,(21-7)!} = {}^{21}C_{7} = \text{R.H.S.}\]
Why: This is exactly the formula with \(n = 21\), \(r = 7\).

Check with numbers
\[{}^{20}C_{7} = 77520,\quad {}^{20}C_{6} = 38760\]
\[77520 + 38760 = 116280\]
\[{}^{21}C_{7} = 116280 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Both sides are the same number. (This is Pascal's rule of Question 14 with \(n = 20\), \(r = 7\).)
